subject: Civil Engineering
title: Evapotranspiration
description: A quick, practical guide to Evapotranspiration.

hook.text: A single oak tree pumps 40,000 gallons of water from the ground to the air each year.

buildup.text: Evapotranspiration combines evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants.

discovery.text: It's the largest water loss in most catchments — often 60% or more of all rainfall.

twist.text: Clearing forests reduces transpiration but increases runoff and erosion — a trade-off.

climax.text: The Penman-Monteith equation estimates ET from weather data — a UNESCO standard.

punchline.text: Most rain never reaches a river. Plants drink it first.

quiz.question: What does evapotranspiration include?
options: Only the evaporation from rivers, lakes, and oceans
Both evaporation from surfaces and water transpired by plants
Only the water absorbed by plant roots for growth

details.summary: Evapotranspiration is the combined loss of water from land surfaces through evaporation from soil and water bodies and transpiration from plants. It typically accounts for 50-70% of precipitation in a watershed and is a critical factor in water balance calculations for agriculture.
details.whyItMatters: Evapotranspiration is the largest water loss in most watersheds. Ignoring or miscalculating it leads to overestimating water available for supply, irrigation, and environmental flows.
takeaways: Evapotranspiration can consume 50-70% of total precipitation in a watershed
The Penman-Monteith equation is the standard method for estimating evapotranspiration
Pan evaporation measurements provide simple field estimates using correction coefficients

faq.question: Why is evapotranspiration so important for water supply engineering?
faq.answer: Reservoir yield depends on inflows minus evaporation losses from the water surface. In arid regions, reservoir evaporation can exceed 2 meters per year, losing enormous volumes. Irrigation demand is essentially crop evapotranspiration minus effective rainfall.

faq.question: How do engineers measure and estimate evapotranspiration?
faq.answer: Direct measurement uses lysimeters or eddy covariance towers. Estimation methods range from simple pan evaporation with correction factors to the physically-based Penman-Monteith equation using temperature, humidity, wind, and solar radiation.
